title: A job queue on Postgres alone
summary: Build a reliable job queue with only PostgreSQL and SKIP LOCKED: workers, retries, dead letters, and enough visibility to debug it.
context: Many teams reach for a message broker long before they need one. Cinder Ledger, a fictional billing company, has Postgres and a deadline, and wants background jobs (invoice documents, reminder drafts, exports) that survive crashes and never run twice at once.
You build the queue as a small library plus a worker. Postgres is the only service: run it locally, in a container or installed. Payloads are fictional invoices for fictional customers.
The interesting work is in the failures: a worker killed mid-job, a job that always fails, a hundred jobs enqueued at once.
must_have: A jobs table and an enqueue call taking a name, a payload, a run-at time and a priority.
Workers that claim jobs with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, plus a test with several workers on one queue showing no job runs twice at once.
Retries with backoff, a maximum-attempts rule, and a dead-letter state that keeps the last error, with a way to requeue a dead job.
Crash safety: a worker that dies mid-job loses its claim after a visibility timeout and the job runs again, shown by a test that kills a worker.
Visibility: a CLI or page with counts by state, the oldest waiting job, the failing job types, and the attempt history of one job.
nice_to_have: An idempotency key so a retried enqueue does not create two jobs.
LISTEN/NOTIFY to wake workers, with polling kept as the fallback.
Graceful shutdown that finishes the current job.
constraints: No paid services, APIs or accounts. A local Postgres only, and no broker, Redis or queue product.
Fictional data only: invoice numbers and customers are made up.
deliverables: A public repo created after you press Start, with commits spread across the window.
A README with how to run it (start Postgres, run a worker, run the tests), what delivery guarantee the queue gives, and what is missing.
judge_focus: Why the claim query is safe, and what a long transaction or a held lock does to it.
How you chose the visibility timeout and what goes wrong if it is too short.
Whether you say plainly if the queue is at-least-once or exactly-once, and what a job author must do about it.
A trail of commits: enqueue and claim first, then each failure mode with its test.
bengaluru_context: Backend and platform teams at Bengaluru SaaS and fintech companies run Postgres-backed queues in production, and interviewers there ask exactly how SKIP LOCKED, retries and dead letters work.
